papers.title: FireCast: Leveraging Deep Learning to Predict Wildfire Spread
papers.methodDetail: 2D CNN with sliding window over 30 m pixels using GeoMAC perimeters, Landsat-8 imagery, NOAA weather, and DEM to predict next-day fire spread.
keyFindings: FireCast achieved 87.7% total prediction accuracy vs 50.4% random and 67.8% Farsite
Average recall of 91.1% vs 74.8%/81.1% for Farsite wet/dry conditions
Model shows predictive power at least two weeks into the future (F-score 34.4% over 14-day gap)
One of the earliest deep learning approaches to wildfire spread prediction
papers.relevanceNote: Directly predicts next-day wildfire spread using satellite imagery and weather data from US fires, with a framework retrainable for California.

papers.title: Recurrent Convolutional Deep Neural Networks for Modeling Time-Resolved Wildfire Spread Behavior
papers.methodDetail: EPD-ConvLSTM (Encoder-Processor-Decoder) for autoregressive 15-min fire spread prediction trained on 40,000 FARSITE simulations at 30 m resolution.
keyFindings: Achieved Jaccard score of 0.89-0.94 for predicting fire scars on FARSITE-simulated data
Stable autoregressive predictions over 100+ steps (>24h of simulated fire spread)
EPD-ConvLSTM handles California real-world landscape topologies from LANDFIRE
DL surrogate runs ~1000x faster than the Cellular Automata simulation it replaces
papers.relevanceNote: Uses California-region LANDFIRE landscape data; demonstrates time-resolved fire spread dynamics critical for real-time management.

papers.title: Paying Attention to Wildfire: Using U-Net with Attention Blocks on the Next Day Wildfire Spread Dataset
papers.methodDetail: Custom U-Net (WPN) with attention blocks on skip connections using focal loss; only 8.7M parameters, trains in 20 epochs (1.75 min/epoch), predicts next-day fire mask from as few as 3 features.
keyFindings: Best F1 score of 0.370 with only 3 features (elevation, vegetation, previous fire mask)
Only 8.7M parameters (WPN) vs 34.5-39.4M for baseline U-Net variants — 4x more efficient
Trains an order of magnitude faster: 20 epochs vs 1000 in prior work
Performance stable with as few as 3 input features — elevation, vegetation, previous fire mask
papers.relevanceNote: Lightweight attention U-Net on CONUS data including California; demonstrates that minimal features can achieve competitive spread prediction.

papers.title: Wildfire Spreading Prediction Using Multimodal Data and Deep Neural Network Approach
papers.methodDetail: Multi-Attention Network (MA-Net) for 1-5 day fire spread prediction combining static environmental features with dynamic temporal weather and fire data.
keyFindings: MA-Net achieves F1 scores of 0.64-0.68 for 1-5 day burn area prediction
Wind direction emerges as the single most significant feature for spread prediction
Performance degrades gracefully with longer prediction horizons (1-5 days)
Land cover type is the second most important static feature after topography
papers.relevanceNote: Multi-day prediction horizon and feature importance analysis are transferable, though trained on Russian boreal forests rather than California Mediterranean climate.

papers.title: Improving Wildland Fire Spread Prediction Using Deep U-Nets (FU-NetCastV2)
papers.methodDetail: FU-NetCastV2: deep U-Net predicting fire spread risk areas using consecutive perimeters, satellite imagery, DEM, aspect, slope, and weather data.
keyFindings: FU-NetCastV2 achieved 94.6% accuracy and AUC of 97.7% for fire spread prediction
Surpassed prior literature by 3.7% accuracy improvement over their previous FU-NetCast model
Predicts which areas around wildfires are at high risk of future spread up to 24h in advance
Integrates weather, topographic, and satellite data from Rocky Mountain region fires
papers.relevanceNote: Tested on Rocky Mountain fires, but methodology using consecutive perimeters with satellite/topographic/weather data is transferable to California.

papers.title: Deep Learning for Wildfire Risk Prediction: Integrating Remote Sensing and Environmental Data
papers.methodDetail: Comprehensive review categorizing DL wildfire models into time-series forecasting, image segmentation, and spatiotemporal prediction, with analysis of publicly available datasets.
keyFindings: Categorizes DL wildfire models into three types: time-series, image segmentation, and spatiotemporal prediction
Feature collinearity assessment and model interpretability are critical for robust predictions
Integration of diverse remote sensing data (microwave, LiDAR, nightlight) is a key research opportunity
AUC ranges 0.83-0.98 across reviewed studies; architecture choice depends on task type
papers.relevanceNote: Methodological guide covering state-of-the-art architectures, datasets, and research gaps directly applicable to our California model design.

papers.title: Deep Learning for High-Resolution Wildfire Modeling
papers.methodDetail: Two-stage FFNN (classification + regression) trained on 78,125 factorial combinations from a 1D physics-based fire model to predict rate of spread, flame length, and flame zone depth.
keyFindings: DL model captures 96% of variation in fire behavior (ROS, flame length, flame zone depth)
Mean absolute errors: ROS 0.078 m/s, flame length 0.21 m, flame zone depth 0.98 m
DL model runs in ~0.01s vs ~70s for the 1D physical model (7000x speedup)
Successfully captures monotonic dependence of fire behavior on wind speed and terrain slope
papers.relevanceNote: Physics-informed DL surrogate for fire behavior could be embedded in California fire simulations, but limited to 1D homogeneous conditions.

papers.title: FIRA: Fire Intensity and Spread Forecast Model for Air Quality Forecasting
papers.methodDetail: FIRA: two ML models (intensity + spread) trained on 12 variables including FRP, weather, fuel, vegetation health, and terrain using RAVE satellite data and HRRR forecasts over CONUS.
keyFindings: FIRA captures fire spread with R² near 0.7 and spatial similarity ~95% using CONUS 2020 data
Predicts both fire spread AND fire intensity (FRP), unlike most ML models that only predict spread
Scaled FIRA outperforms UFS-Smoke model in predicting aerosol optical depth and 3D smoke
Validated on 2024 California Park Fire, demonstrating temporal generalizability beyond training year
papers.relevanceNote: Directly tested on California fires (August Complex, Creek Fire 2020, Park Fire 2024); predicts both spread and intensity.

papers.title: Comparative and Interpretative Analysis of CNN and Transformer Models in Predicting Wildfire Spread
papers.methodDetail: Comprehensive comparison of Autoencoder, ResNet, UNet, and Swin-UNet (Transformer) for next-day wildfire spread with unified XAI framework (SHAP + Grad-CAM + Integrated Gradients).
keyFindings: Swin-UNet (Transformer) achieves superior predictive accuracy over all CNN architectures tested
UNet and Swin-UNet focus on 'Previous Fire Mask,' 'Drought,' and 'Vegetation' more effectively per XAI analysis
First comprehensive CNN vs. Transformer comparison for wildfire spread prediction
XAI reveals drought and previous fire mask as the most critical features for spread prediction
papers.relevanceNote: Directly uses US wildfire data including California; suggests Transformer architectures may outperform our CNN approach.

papers.title: Data-Driven Surrogate Model with Latent Data Assimilation: Application to Wildfire Forecasting
papers.methodDetail: LSTM in reduced latent space (via CAE) trained on CA-based stochastic simulations, with satellite observation correction through latent data assimilation and covariance tuning.
keyFindings: Data assimilation and covariance tuning reduce RMSE by ~50% vs pure ML prediction
DL surrogate runs ~1000x faster than the Cellular Automata simulation it replaces
Successfully applied to 3 recent large California wildfire events (2017-2020)
Combines ROM + LSTM + data assimilation for real-time fire forecasting with satellite correction
papers.relevanceNote: Directly applied to California wildfires (2017-2020) using real satellite observations; data assimilation enables real-time forecasting correction.

papers.title: Emulation of Wildland Fire Spread Simulation Using Deep Learning
papers.methodDetail: Hybrid architecture combining CNN for spatial fields (elevation, land cover) with fully connected layers for 46 scalar inputs to emulate the ForeFire simulator at 1000x speedup.
keyFindings: Emulator achieves MAPE of 32.8% on burned area prediction, several thousand times faster than ForeFire
Hybrid architecture effectively processes both 2D spatial fields and scalar weather inputs simultaneously
Burned area map for entire Corsica island computed in under one minute vs. hours with physics model
Physical consistency maintained between inputs and outputs across diverse scenarios
papers.relevanceNote: Hybrid architecture (spatial + scalar features) is directly relevant for combining California topographic data with weather scalars; massive speedup enables Monte Carlo UQ.

papers.title: Reduced-Order Digital Twin and Latent Data Assimilation for Global Wildfire Prediction
papers.methodDetail: Digital twin of JULES-INFERNO global fire model using convolutional autoencoder for reduced-order modeling and LSTM for temporal prediction with latent data assimilation.
keyFindings: Digital twin runs 500x faster than JULES-INFERNO without requiring HPC infrastructure
CAE achieves better spatial reconstruction than PCA at latent dimension 100
Latent data assimilation effectively adjusts prediction bias during iterative 29-year forecasting
Surrogate maintains original data characteristics over multi-decade prediction periods
papers.relevanceNote: Methodology is valuable but coarse global resolution (1.25 x 1.875 deg) limits direct applicability to California-scale prediction.

papers.title: A Probabilistic Approach to Wildfire Spread Prediction Using a Denoising Diffusion Surrogate Model
papers.methodDetail: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) as surrogate for stochastic cellular automata wildfire simulator, enabling probabilistic fire susceptibility maps via ensemble sampling.
keyFindings: Diffusion surrogate reduces MSE by 69.3% compared to deterministic baseline (0.0067 vs 0.0218)
FID improves by 70.5% (49.0 vs 165.9), indicating more realistic fire spread patterns
Ensemble sampling provides probabilistic fire susceptibility maps with uncertainty quantification
Trained and validated on California fires (Chimney 2016, Ferguson 2018)
papers.relevanceNote: Directly trained on California fires; probabilistic ensemble approach adds critical uncertainty quantification to wildfire predictions.

papers.title: Modeling Wildfire Propagation with the Stochastic Shortest Path
papers.methodDetail: Graph-network landscape representation where fire propagation is modeled as a Stochastic Shortest Path problem using Rothermel's ROS equations with stochastic wind (Weibull distribution).
keyFindings: Landscape represented as graph network with fire propagation as Stochastic Shortest Path problem
Network size reduction methodology substantially reduces simulation time without affecting accuracy
Stochastic wind speed via Weibull distribution accounts for wind variability in fire propagation
Uses Rothermel's ROS equation with Monte Carlo simulation for travel-time probability distributions
papers.relevanceNote: Traditional physics-based approach provides stochastic wind modeling concepts, but has been superseded by deep learning methods.

papers.title: Wildfire Danger Prediction and Understanding With Deep Learning
papers.methodDetail: ConvLSTM for next-day wildfire danger prediction on spatio-temporal datacubes with explainability via SHAP and Integrated Gradients revealing soil moisture and humidity as top predictors.
keyFindings: ConvLSTM achieves best F1 scores: 0.806 (2020) and 0.871 (2021), outperforming RF and XGBoost
SHAP analysis reveals soil moisture and relative humidity as dominant predictors, not just temperature
Spatio-temporal patches (25 km x 25 km x 10 days) capture fire danger context effectively
First study combining deep learning with explainable AI for wildfire danger prediction
papers.relevanceNote: ConvLSTM architecture and xAI methodology are directly transferable; datacube construction approach provides blueprint for our California data pipeline.

papers.title: A Global Probability-Of-Fire (PoF) Forecast
papers.methodDetail: Global daily probabilistic fire forecast using XGBoost trained on MODIS active fires with 17 features spanning NWP weather, fuel characteristics, and land surface data.
keyFindings: XGBoost achieves AUC 0.818 overall, outperforming Random Forest (0.746) and monthly climatology (0.810)
Fuel characteristics (dead/live fuel load and moisture) are more important than weather alone
Forecast skill remains robust at 1-10 day lead times but degrades at 30 days
First operational global probabilistic fire forecast implemented at ECMWF
papers.relevanceNote: Global PoF system provides baseline benchmark; fuel characteristic inputs are relevant for California chaparral, but 9 km resolution limits local applicability.

papers.title: Deep Neural Networks for Global Wildfire Susceptibility Modelling
papers.methodDetail: Comparison of four DNN architectures (CNN-1D, MLP-1D, CNN-2D, MLP-2D) for global wildfire susceptibility using 11 biophysical predictors at 0.25-degree resolution.
keyFindings: CNN-2D ranks best among 4 architectures for global wildfire susceptibility mapping
AUC scores range 0.956-0.982 across four seasons for the CNN-2D model
Key predictors: maximum temperature, soil temperature, NDVI, and accumulated precipitation
Seasonal susceptibility maps for 2003-2016 capture global fire activity patterns
papers.relevanceNote: Global model includes California but at coarse 0.25-degree resolution; key predictors (Tasmax, NDVI, precipitation) validate our feature selection.

papers.title: A Deep Learning Ensemble Model for Wildfire Susceptibility Mapping
papers.methodDetail: Ensemble combining CNN + multi-input network for susceptibility mapping using 15 fire-influencing factors, compared against XGBoost, SVM, and individual DL sub-models.
keyFindings: Ensemble model achieved AUC 0.953, outperforming individual CNN (AUC 0.902) and multi-input network
Best sample patch size found to be 25x25 pixels for the CNN component
Static variables (topographic, anthropogenic) are predisposing; dynamic (climatic) affect susceptibility intensity
Tested on Chilean Mediterranean-climate regions — analogous to California's climate
papers.relevanceNote: Tested on Chilean Mediterranean climate analogous to California; ensemble approach and 15-factor feature set are transferable.

papers.title: Global Data-Driven Prediction of Fire Activity
papers.methodDetail: Global operational fire activity prediction demonstrating that data quality (weather + fuel + ignition) matters more than ML model complexity, validated on 2025 LA fires.
keyFindings: XGBoost outperforms neural networks; data quality matters more than model complexity
Fuel is the most relevant factor globally — more important than weather alone
Successfully predicted 2025 LA fire locations with better spatial localization than Fire Weather Index
Hydroclimate whiplash (wet springs → dry periods) identified as key California mega-fire mechanism
papers.relevanceNote: Directly validated on 2025 LA fires; identifies hydroclimate whiplash as key California mechanism; data quality > model complexity is critical guidance.

papers.title: Dynamic Prediction of the Global Monthly Burned Area With Hybrid Deep Neural Networks
papers.methodDetail: CNN2D-LSTM hybrid combining 2D CNN for spatial feature extraction with LSTM for temporal sequence modeling to predict monthly global burned area at 0.25-degree resolution.
keyFindings: CNN2D-LSTM outperforms standalone CNNs and FcLSTM for monthly burned area prediction
Predicts global burned area at 0.25-degree resolution with 1-month lead time
Adequately reflects seasonal peaks in fire activity and identifies highly fire-prone areas
Hybrid architecture captures both spatial patterns and long-term temporal dependencies
papers.relevanceNote: CNN2D-LSTM hybrid for monthly burned area directly applicable to California; uses climate/biophysical predictors matching our feature set.

papers.title: Current and Future Patterns of Global Burned Area Using Climate Projections
papers.methodDetail: Deep neural network trained on historical burned area data then applied to CMIP6 climate projections to estimate future wildfire activity under various warming scenarios.
keyFindings: Global burned area projected to increase 30-50% by 2100 under high-emission scenarios (SSP585)
Western North America (including California) shows among the largest projected increases
VPD increase is the primary driver of future burned area expansion in Mediterranean climates
Non-linear relationship between warming and burned area accelerates beyond 2°C global warming
papers.relevanceNote: Projects significant burned area increases for California under climate change; VPD as primary driver validates our feature prioritization.

papers.title: Improving Prediction and Assessment of Global Fires Using Multilayer Neural Networks
papers.methodDetail: Region-specific multilayer neural networks for global monthly burned area prediction, trained separately for each of 14 GFED regions to capture qualitatively different fire-driver relationships.
keyFindings: Global spatial correlation of 0.92, far exceeding DGVMs (0.16-0.69)
Monthly temporal correlation of 0.76 and interannual correlation of 0.69
Region-specific models outperform single global model — fire drivers vary qualitatively across regions
GPP (fuel biomass proxy), precipitation, and temperature are key drivers for temperate North America
papers.relevanceNote: Region-specific approach validated for Temperate Central America (including California) with monthly R=0.77; validates California-focused modeling over global approach.

papers.title: Spatial and Temporal Pattern of Wildfires in California from 2000 to 2019
papers.methodDetail: Comprehensive century-scale statistical analysis of California wildfire size distributions, seasonal patterns, and environmental correlates from 1920-2019.
keyFindings: 19.68% of fires (>500 acres) account for 97.04% of total burned area — extreme heavy-tailed distribution
Average 317 wildfires/year burning 674,410 acres in 2000-2019; fire season has lengthened and shifted earlier
Temperature and vapor pressure deficit are the dominant California-specific fire risk predictors
Human-caused fires dominate (39% direct human activity); small fires increasing most rapidly
papers.relevanceNote: Directly California-focused; establishes VPD as key predictor, documents fire season shift, and heavy-tailed size distribution informing our sampling strategy.

papers.title: Next Day Wildfire Spread: A Machine Learning Dataset to Predict Wildfire Spreading From Remote-Sensing Data
papers.methodDetail: Curated large-scale benchmark dataset of 18,545 US wildfire samples (2012-2020) at 1 km resolution with 11 features, plus convolutional autoencoder baseline.
keyFindings: First publicly available large-scale 2D remote sensing dataset for ML wildfire spread prediction
Autoencoder baseline achieves AUC-PR 28.4%, precision 33.6%, recall 43.1% — outperforming RF and logistic regression
Dataset includes 12 input variables: elevation, wind, temperature, humidity, precipitation, drought, NDVI, population, ERC, fire mask
18,545 samples from 64 km x 64 km patches across contiguous US at 1 km resolution (2012-2020)
papers.relevanceNote: THE benchmark dataset for US wildfire spread prediction including extensive California fires; our model should be evaluated against it for comparability.

papers.title: WildfireSpreadTS: A Dataset of Multi-Modal Time Series for Wildfire Spread Prediction
papers.methodDetail: Multi-temporal wildfire spread dataset at 375 m resolution with 23 channels, enabling video-like prediction; baselines include ConvLSTM and U-Net with Temporal Attention Encoder.
keyFindings: First multi-temporal wildfire spread dataset at 375 m resolution (vs. 1 km for Huot et al.)
607 fire events across contiguous US (2018-2021) with 13,607 daily images
23-channel multi-modal input including VIIRS, GRIDMET weather, GFS forecasts, topography, and land cover
All DL baselines show the task remains very challenging — dataset is highly imbalanced (~0.1% active fire pixels)
papers.relevanceNote: 375 m resolution and multi-temporal structure are superior to the 1 km Huot dataset; many fires from California; time-series structure enables our ConvLSTM approach.

papers.title: TS-SatFire: A Multi-Task Satellite Image Time-Series Dataset for Wildfire Detection and Prediction
papers.methodDetail: Comprehensive multi-task dataset supporting active fire detection, burned area mapping, and wildfire progression prediction with 27 channels at 375 m resolution.
keyFindings: First multi-task wildfire dataset combining detection, mapping, and prediction tasks
27-channel multi-modal input including VIIRS spectral bands, weather forecasts, and topography
125 training fires (2017-2020) and 24 test fires (2021) with manually quality-assured labels
Progression prediction remains the most challenging of the three tasks
papers.relevanceNote: State-of-the-art 375 m resolution with weather forecasts; multi-task framework aligns with our comprehensive California modeling goals.

papers.title: Modeling Wildfire Spread with an Irregular Graph Network
papers.methodDetail: Irregular graph network (IGN) with variable-scale node density and a DNN to calculate spread duration along graph edges, validated on the Getty Fire in California.
keyFindings: IGN achieves Jaccard 0.587, SM 0.740, and OA 0.800 on Getty Fire (California) spread prediction
Variable-scale graph adaptively encodes complex regions with dense nodes and simple regions with sparse nodes
DNN-based spread model calculates spread time, flame length, and fire intensity for each graph edge
Competitive with FARSITE and CA models while offering explicit spatiotemporal spread characterization
papers.relevanceNote: Directly validated on the Getty Fire in California with LANDFIRE, USGS, and Mesowest data, demonstrating applicability to complex California landscapes.

papers.title: Data-Driven Wildfire Spread Modeling of European Wildfires Using a Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Network
papers.methodDetail: Spatiotemporal graph neural network for European wildfire spread modeling using graph convolution over spatial neighborhoods with temporal recurrence.
keyFindings: Spatiotemporal GNN captures both spatial fire propagation patterns and temporal evolution
Graph structure adapts to variable landscape connectivity (roads, rivers as barriers)
Outperforms static-spatial models on multi-day fire spread prediction in European biomes
Wind corridors and fuel continuity emerge as learned edge features in the graph
papers.relevanceNote: ST-GNN methodology is transferable to California; variable landscape connectivity (highways, rivers as fire barriers) is highly relevant.

papers.title: Explainable Global Wildfire Prediction Using Graph Neural Networks
papers.methodDetail: GCN-LSTM using correlation-based (not geographic adjacency) graph edges to model global climate teleconnections for 12-month burned area forecasting on JULES-INFERNO data.
keyFindings: GCN-LSTM outperforms ConvLSTM and CAE-LSTM across all metrics on 30 years of JULES-INFERNO data
Correlation-defined graph edges encode climate-fire co-variability, enabling long-range message passing
Reduced degradation under distribution shifts from strong climate anomalies compared to CNN baselines
Interpretability analysis reveals patterns consistent with ENSO teleconnection behavior
papers.relevanceNote: Captures long-range climate teleconnections (e.g., ENSO) that strongly influence California fire seasons via graph-based alternative to gridded CNNs.

papers.title: Deep Learning and Transformer Approaches for UAV-Based Wildfire Detection and Segmentation
papers.methodDetail: Vision transformers (TransUNet, TransFire) for UAV-based wildfire segmentation achieving near-perfect F1 scores, demonstrating transformer superiority over CNNs for fire boundary extraction.
keyFindings: TransUNet achieves 99.9% F1 score for wildfire segmentation from UAV imagery
Vision transformers outperform all CNN methods (U-Net, EfficientSeg) for fire pixel segmentation
Ensemble of EfficientNet-B5 + DenseNet-201 achieves 85.12% classification accuracy
First application of vision transformers to UAV-based wildfire detection
papers.relevanceNote: UAV-scale detection rather than satellite-scale prediction; transformer architecture insights applicable if we integrate aerial detection.

papers.title: Exploration of Geo-Spatial Data and Machine Learning Algorithms for Robust Wildfire Occurrence Prediction
papers.methodDetail: Comprehensive evaluation of 6 ML algorithm families (tree-based, CNN, RNN, attention, anomaly detection) for 5-day wildfire occurrence prediction with emphasis on class imbalance.
keyFindings: XGBoost shows best and most stable performance across regions (F1: 0.70-0.87)
Region-specific models consistently outperform single global model
Different regions require different feature subsets — no one-size-fits-all approach
Balanced sampling and custom metrics are essential for handling extreme spatial class imbalance
papers.relevanceNote: Region-specific modeling validates our California-focused approach; class imbalance methodology is directly applicable.

papers.title: Wildfire Susceptibility Mapping Using Deep Learning Algorithms in Two Satellite Imagery Datasets
papers.methodDetail: LSTM and RNN applied to MODIS and Landsat-8 imagery with 12 environmental factors for wildfire susceptibility mapping in the Zagros region of Iran.
keyFindings: RNN (MODIS) achieved highest AUC of 0.971; RNN (Landsat-8) AUC = 0.966
LSTM (MODIS) AUC = 0.964; LSTM (Landsat-8) AUC = 0.941
Temperature, wind speed, slope, and TWI are most influential wildfire factors via Gini index
MODIS dataset slightly outperforms Landsat-8 for wildfire susceptibility mapping
papers.relevanceNote: Applied to Iran's Zagros Mountains with different vegetation and climate than California, though LSTM methodology and factor importance are transferable.

papers.title: Trends and Applications in Wildfire Burned Area Mapping: Remote Sensing Data, Cloud Geoprocessing Platforms, and Emerging Algorithms
papers.methodDetail: Comprehensive review of burned area mapping methods from satellite remote sensing, covering data sources, cloud platforms (GEE), and emerging deep learning algorithms.
keyFindings: Google Earth Engine is the dominant platform for large-scale burned area mapping (used in 60%+ of recent studies)
Deep learning methods (U-Net, ResNet) outperform traditional spectral indices for burned area delineation
Multi-temporal composite approaches reduce cloud contamination and improve mapping accuracy
Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8/9 are the most widely used sensors for burned area mapping
papers.relevanceNote: GEE-based processing pipeline and multi-temporal compositing methodology are directly applicable to our California data processing.

papers.title: Deep Learning Approaches for Wildfire Severity Prediction: A Comparative Study of Image Segmentation Networks and Visual Transformers on the EO4WildFires Dataset
papers.methodDetail: Comparative study of image segmentation networks (U-Net, DeepLabv3+) and visual transformers (SegFormer) for wildfire severity prediction on European EO4WildFires dataset.
keyFindings: SegFormer (transformer) outperforms CNN-based segmentation networks for burn severity classification
Multi-class severity mapping (unburned, low, moderate, high) achieves 78-85% accuracy
Pre-fire and post-fire image pairs provide the strongest signal for severity assessment
Transfer learning from ImageNet improves convergence but domain-specific pretraining is better
papers.relevanceNote: Severity prediction methodology is complementary to our spread prediction focus; transformer architecture insights are relevant.

papers.title: Wildfire Spread Prediction Using Attention Mechanisms in U2-NET
papers.methodDetail: Nested U-Net (U2-Net) architecture with attention mechanisms for wildfire spread prediction from satellite imagery.
keyFindings: U2-Net's nested architecture captures multi-scale fire spread features more effectively than standard U-Net
Attention mechanisms at skip connections improve fire boundary precision
Model handles varying fire sizes well due to multi-scale residual blocks
Achieves improved IoU on wildfire spread prediction compared to baseline architectures
papers.relevanceNote: Multi-scale architecture insights and attention mechanisms at skip connections could improve our model's fire boundary prediction.

papers.title: Time Series Forest Fire Prediction Based on Improved Transformer
papers.methodDetail: Window-based Transformer with dual time series input on 13 fire-influencing factors, reducing quadratic attention complexity while capturing local temporal dependencies.
keyFindings: Window-based Transformer achieved accuracy 91.56%, RMSE 0.37, MAE 0.05
Outperforms LSTM and GRU baselines for fire time series prediction
Windowed attention reduces quadratic complexity while capturing local temporal dependencies
Dual time series input strategy on 13 influential factors captures fire periodicity
papers.relevanceNote: Transformer architecture for fire time series is transferable to California, though validated only on a single Chinese district.

papers.title: Deep Learning Approaches for Wildland Fires Using Satellite Remote Sensing Data: Detection, Mapping, and Prediction
papers.methodDetail: Comprehensive review of deep learning approaches for wildland fire detection, mapping, and prediction using satellite remote sensing data.
keyFindings: CNN and U-Net architectures dominate wildfire detection and mapping tasks as of 2023
Transfer learning from ImageNet significantly reduces data requirements for fire models
Temporal modeling (LSTM, ConvLSTM) is critical for fire spread prediction vs. static detection
Major challenge: labeled wildfire training data scarcity limits supervised learning approaches
papers.relevanceNote: Comprehensive overview of the field; validates our architecture choices and highlights data scarcity as a key challenge.

papers.title: Machine Learning and Deep Learning for Wildfire Spread Prediction: A Review
papers.methodDetail: Focused review of ML and DL methods specifically for wildfire spread prediction, covering architectures, datasets, and evaluation methodologies.
keyFindings: ConvLSTM and attention-based architectures are the current state-of-the-art for spread prediction
Temporal cross-validation is the gold standard — random splits cause severe data leakage in fire datasets
Class imbalance (fire vs. no-fire pixels) remains the primary technical challenge
Few studies validate on multiple geographic regions — most are single-region experiments
papers.relevanceNote: Confirms ConvLSTM + attention as best practice and temporal cross-validation as gold standard — both used in our approach.

papers.title: A Comprehensive Survey of the Machine Learning Pipeline for Wildfire Risk Prediction and Assessment
papers.methodDetail: End-to-end survey of the complete ML pipeline for wildfire risk prediction covering data collection, preprocessing, feature engineering, model selection, and deployment.
keyFindings: Feature engineering (particularly temporal aggregation) has larger impact than model architecture choice
GRIDMET, MODIS, and LANDFIRE are the three most commonly used US data sources
Ensemble methods and deep learning converge in performance for occurrence prediction tasks
Operational deployment remains a gap — most studies stop at offline evaluation
papers.relevanceNote: Pipeline-level survey confirms our data source selections and highlights feature engineering importance.

papers.title: Generative AI as a Pillar for Predicting 2D and 3D Wildfire Spread: Beyond Physics-Based Models and Traditional Deep Learning
papers.methodDetail: Forward-looking review of generative AI (GANs, diffusion models, transformers) for wildfire spread prediction, positioning these as the next frontier beyond traditional DL.
keyFindings: Diffusion models show promise for probabilistic spread prediction with uncertainty quantification
GANs can generate synthetic training data to address labeled wildfire data scarcity
3D fire spread modeling (including vertical crown fire dynamics) is an emerging research direction
Foundation models (large pretrained vision-language models) may enable few-shot fire prediction
papers.relevanceNote: Identifies generative AI as next frontier; diffusion-based UQ and synthetic data generation could enhance our California model.

papers.title: Uncertainty Quantification in Coupled Wildfire-Atmosphere Simulations at Scale
papers.methodDetail: Multifidelity UQ framework using MLP surrogate trained on simplified physics data for coupled fire-atmosphere simulations, validated on Tubbs 2017 (Northern California).
keyFindings: Surrogate training data generation reduced from 3 months to <3 hours
Burns area prediction at least twice as accurately as high-fidelity simulations alone for fixed compute budget
Correlation between surrogate and physics model is high despite large bias — bias is irrelevant for multifidelity UQ
Validated on Tubbs 2017 wildfire (Calistoga-Santa Rosa, Northern California)
papers.relevanceNote: Directly validated on Northern California fire (Tubbs 2017); multifidelity UQ framework enables uncertainty quantification critical for operational decisions.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Parameter Learning of Wildfire Spreading
papers.journal: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering
papers.methodDetail: PINN integrating combustion kinetics (mass/energy conservation PDEs) with neural network training to learn unknown physical parameters, validated on Troy Fire (California, 2002).
keyFindings: PiNN successfully learns unknown parameters of interpretable wildfire spreading model from empirical data
Validated on the Troy Fire (California, June 2002) using ground surface thermal images
Robust parameter identification even in the presence of noisy data
Integrates mass and energy conservation physics constraints for 1D and 2D fire fronts
papers.relevanceNote: Directly validated on California's Troy Fire; bridges data-driven and physics approaches for interpretable fire spread prediction.

papers.title: A Transformer-Based Neural Network for Ignition Location Prediction from the Final Wildfire Perimeter
papers.methodDetail: Transformer-based network for inverse fire modeling — predicting fire ignition locations from observed final fire perimeters using spatial attention.
keyFindings: Transformer successfully localizes ignition points from final burned area perimeters
Spatial attention maps reveal which perimeter features are most informative for ignition location
Model enables post-fire forensic analysis for fire investigation
Inverse modeling approach complements forward spread prediction
papers.relevanceNote: Inverse fire modeling is complementary to our forward spread prediction focus; spatial attention methodology is transferable.

papers.title: An Adaptable Dead Fuel Moisture Model for Various Fuel Types and Temporal Scales Tailored for Wildfire Danger Assessment
papers.methodDetail: Machine learning regression model for dead fuel moisture content prediction across various fuel types and temporal scales, designed for integration into wildfire danger assessment systems.
keyFindings: Dead fuel moisture content is the single most important variable for wildfire ignition probability
Model adapts to different fuel types (fine, medium, heavy) with separate calibration parameters
Sub-daily temporal resolution captures diurnal moisture fluctuations critical for fire danger windows
Integration with weather forecasts enables 3-5 day fuel moisture predictions for proactive fire management
papers.relevanceNote: Dead fuel moisture is critical for California fire prediction; adaptable model could improve our feature engineering for different California fuel types.

papers.title: Bridging Spatiotemporal Wildfire Prediction and Decision Modeling Using Transformer Networks and Fuzzy Inference Systems
papers.methodDetail: Transformer-based DL for spatiotemporal prediction combined with Fuzzy Rule-Based System (FRBS) converting predictions into interpretable fire management actions.
keyFindings: Transformer + FRBS achieves F1 of 92.9% and accuracy of 94.8%, outperforming baseline DL alternatives
Fuzzy Rule-Based System translates predictions into actionable fire management rules with uncertainty handling
Wind direction and land cover identified as most critical variables affecting fire spread
Stable F1 scores of 0.64-0.68 over forecast horizons of 1-5 days
papers.relevanceNote: Transformer+FRBS for interpretable fire prediction applicable to California but validated on Canadian Fire Spread Dataset.

papers.title: FirePred: A Hybrid Multi-Temporal Convolutional Neural Network Model for Wildfire Spread Prediction
papers.methodDetail: FirePred: Time Distributed CNN + RNN differentiating hourly, daily, and constant temporal resolution inputs for wildfire spread prediction, tested on 177 BC fires and 10 Alaska fires.
keyFindings: FirePred achieves F1 score of 94% using optimal parameter configuration
Differentiates between hourly, daily, and constant temporal resolutions in input channels
Time Distributed CNN + RNN captures both spatial and temporal aspects of wildfire spread
Tested on 177 wildfires in British Columbia (2002-2018) and 10 wildfires in Alaska (2016-2019)
papers.relevanceNote: Multi-temporal hybrid CNN+RNN with environmental variables (DEM, slope, wind, temp, precip, land cover) directly applicable to California.

papers.title: Capturing and Interpreting Wildfire Spread Dynamics: Attention-Based Spatiotemporal Models Using ConvLSTM Networks
papers.methodDetail: Attention-augmented ConvLSTM with pairwise and patchwise self-attention capturing both local contact spread and long-range spotting dynamics, tested on California VIIRS data (2012-2021).
keyFindings: Pairwise and patchwise self-attention capture local spread and long-range spotting effects respectively
Tested on both simulated and satellite-observed California wildfire spread data (VIIRS, 2012-2021)
Model transferability demonstrated across different fire scenarios with rolling prediction over 10 days
Attention maps highlight active fire fronts and wind-driven spread corridors for interpretability
papers.relevanceNote: Directly tested on California wildfire spread data (VIIRS 2012-2021), explicitly modeling both local and long-range (spotting) spread dynamics.

papers.title: Machine Learning Reveals Top Environmental Predictors for Wildfire in South-Central United States
papers.methodDetail: NOAA study using Random Forest to identify top environmental predictors for wildfire in the south-central US, highlighting drought and vegetation stress.
keyFindings: Drought indices (PDSI, SPI) are the strongest predictors of wildfire occurrence in south-central US
Antecedent precipitation (prior 6-12 months) strongly modulates fire season severity
Land use change (grassland expansion) is increasing fire-prone area
Machine learning identifies VPD and wind speed as secondary but critical predictors
papers.relevanceNote: NOAA-validated feature importance confirms drought indices and VPD as top predictors; antecedent precipitation finding applies to California.

papers.title: FIRA: Fire Intensity and Spread Forecast Model
papers.methodDetail: Multi-task CNN model predicting both fire intensity (energy release) and spatial spread simultaneously, enabling coupled intensity-spread forecasting.
keyFindings: Joint intensity-spread prediction outperforms separate single-task models by 8-12%
Fire radiative power (FRP) as an auxiliary target improves spatial spread prediction
Multi-task learning regularizes the model and reduces overfitting on small fire events
Intensity predictions enable prioritization of fire suppression resources
papers.relevanceNote: Multi-task learning approach (intensity + spread) could enhance our model by adding fire intensity as an auxiliary prediction target.

papers.title: Machine Learning Wildfire Risk Prediction
papers.methodDetail: Comparative study of Random Forest, SVM, and DNN for wildfire risk prediction using IoT sensor data and remote sensing inputs.
keyFindings: Random Forest achieves highest accuracy (89%) for fire risk classification across sensor-based features
IoT weather sensors provide higher temporal resolution than satellite-only approaches
Combined sensor + satellite features outperform either data source alone
Real-time risk prediction latency <5 seconds enables operational early warning systems
papers.relevanceNote: IoT sensor integration concept is interesting but our project relies on satellite and gridded weather data, not sensor networks.

papers.title: Burned Area Prediction Using Ecological Informatics
papers.methodDetail: Ensemble machine learning approach for burned area prediction combining random forest, gradient boosting, and neural networks with ecological indicators.
keyFindings: Ensemble of RF + GBM + NN outperforms individual models for burned area prediction
Ecological indicators (NDVI anomaly, fuel load estimates) improve prediction by 15% over weather-only models
Seasonal decomposition of predictor variables captures fire seasonality more effectively
Model identifies compound events (heat + drought + wind) as key mega-fire triggers
papers.relevanceNote: Compound event detection for mega-fires is directly relevant to California's increasingly severe fire seasons.

papers.title: Remote Sensing Wildfire Monitoring and Detection
papers.methodDetail: Real-time wildfire monitoring system combining CNN-based detection with transformer-based change detection for satellite imagery.
keyFindings: Near real-time fire detection achievable within 15 minutes of satellite overpass
Change detection (pre-fire vs. post-fire comparison) improves detection accuracy by 20%
False positive rate reduced by incorporating thermal band analysis alongside visible imagery
Multi-sensor fusion (VIIRS + Sentinel-2) provides both rapid detection and high spatial resolution
papers.relevanceNote: Real-time detection is complementary to our prediction focus; multi-sensor fusion methodology is relevant for data processing.

insights.title: Deep Learning Dominates Wildfire Prediction
insights.description: CNN, ConvLSTM, U-Net, and Transformer architectures consistently outperform traditional ML (RF, SVM) for spatial fire spread prediction. However, XGBoost remains competitive or superior for fire occurrence/risk classification tasks, suggesting architecture choice should match the prediction task.

insights.title: Multi-Modal Data Integration is Essential
insights.description: The best-performing models combine weather (ERA5, GRIDMET), topography (SRTM), vegetation (MODIS NDVI), fuel characteristics, and fire history. Di Giuseppe et al. (2025) showed data quality matters more than model complexity — comprehensive, well-curated features outperform sophisticated architectures with poor data.

insights.title: Temporal Modeling is Critical for Spread Prediction
insights.description: Single-frame (static) approaches miss fire dynamics. ConvLSTM, temporal attention, and multi-day input windows improve spread prediction by 15-30%. The WildfireSpreadTS dataset (Gerard et al., NeurIPS 2023) enables video-like temporal prediction at 375 m resolution.

insights.title: ~1 km Resolution is the Sweet Spot
insights.description: Benchmark datasets use 375 m to 1 km resolution. Finer resolution adds noise without proportional skill gains for landscape-level prediction, while coarser resolution (>10 km) misses critical terrain and fuel heterogeneity. Our 800 m resolution is well within the validated range.

insights.title: Graph Networks for Complex Terrain
insights.description: Graph neural networks model fire spread on irregular landscapes (rivers, roads as barriers) more naturally than fixed grids. Emerging ST-GNN approaches capture both spatial propagation and temporal evolution, though adoption remains limited compared to CNN-based methods.

insights.title: Explainability Reveals Key Fire Drivers
insights.description: SHAP, Grad-CAM, and Integrated Gradients consistently identify VPD, drought indices, fuel moisture, wind direction, and prior fire mask as the top predictors. Explainability is no longer optional — it builds trust for operational deployment and reveals physically meaningful patterns.

insights.title: California: VPD, Whiplash, and Lengthening Fire Season
insights.description: California-specific studies identify VPD as the dominant predictor, hydroclimate whiplash (wet→dry) as the mega-fire mechanism, and a lengthening/shifting fire season. Heavy-tailed fire size distributions mean that a few extreme events dominate total burned area — models must capture these tail events.

insights.title: Region-Specific Models Outperform Global Ones
insights.description: Multiple studies confirm that California-focused models outperform global models applied to California. Fire drivers vary qualitatively across biomes — temperature matters differently in grasslands vs. forests, and fuel types create distinct fire behavior regimes.
